source.title: Interpreting Adaptive Gradient Methods by Parameter Scaling for Learning-Rate-Free Optimization

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper through its convergence-analysis appendix; no relevant truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Its own results show that learning-rate-free methods can overfit, and that their test accuracy varies with optimizer and task; however, it does not test the listed memorization, width, architecture, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-measure, or memorized-example-removal claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports optimizer comparisons on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, ADE20K, STL-10 and reinforcement-learning tasks, including test metrics and training loss for CIFAR-100. These outcomes bear on V4's optimizer/generalization relationship, but the experiments primarily evaluate learning-rate-free methods and do not isolate adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers under the limited-tuning conditions in V4. Cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Table 3 includes SGD and Adam baselines on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, so its results bear on V4. The record omitted those SGD comparisons. The paper does not document V4's restricted tuning protocol, and several poor outcomes reflect optimization failure rather than demonstrated overfitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors interpret adaptive gradients as steepest descent on parameter-scaled networks and introduce PS-SPS and PS-DA-SGD to extend learning-rate-free optimization across tasks. They emphasize PS-DA-SGD's robustness and performance, while acknowledging stronger overfitting on small datasets and proposing regularization or sharpness-aware optimization as future remedies.
record.recipe_differences: Optimizer comparisons focused on adapting learning-rate-free methods to Adam-style parameter scaling; used task-specific experiments rather than the version's limited-tuning adaptive-versus-SGD comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and model affect optimizer performance; enabling weight decay narrows the reported performance gap. In VGG-19 without batch normalization, learning-rate-free methods show lower accuracy primarily due to overfitting. In self-supervised STL-10, larger estimated learning rates accompany better performance for some methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay narrows accuracy differences among adaptive learning-rate-free methods and AdamW.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization can improve the relative performance of learning-rate-free adaptive optimizers.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive learning-rate estimation methods differ in semantic-segmentation fine-tuning, with overly large estimated rates associated with worse performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate-free optimizer performance depends on the downstream task and estimated step size.

fits_no_version.finding: Prodigy and PS-SPS outperform D-Adapt Adam and PS-DA-SGD in the reported self-supervised experiment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger estimated learning rates can accompany better downstream accuracy in small-data self-supervised learning.

record.problems: No explicit uncertainty estimates are given for the reported accuracy and reward values. The CIFAR-100 results include train loss, but most evaluations do not report training performance, so a training-test gap is not directly measured. Experiments compare methods with different learning-rate procedures, and do not isolate V4's limited-tuning conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results were left out.

record.verdict_notes: Verdicts use the supplied text, including omitted SGD baselines. The study is not an original source for V4. Its optimizer ordering provides evidence, but the paper does not establish that its tuning budget matches V4's limited-tuning condition. Poor held-out performance alone is not evidence of overfitting when training performance is unavailable.

Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.

Magnitude-aware sharpness measurement and comparison to other generalization measures.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizer test accuracy; CIFAR-100 top-1 test accuracy with train loss in parentheses.
rows.measure: Top-1 test accuracy; train loss in parentheses
rows.note: The table is flattened, but its method rows and the nearby paragraph identify this ResNet-32/CIFAR-100 result set. The comparison is among learning-rate-free methods and hand-tuned Adam; it does not establish the limited-tuning adaptive-versus-SGD claim.
rows.check: Missing SGD baseline: 66.7% accuracy, training loss 0.233. Adam achieves higher accuracy, 68.3%, whereas the other recorded adaptive methods achieve 50.1–66.4%. These are mixed outcomes, not a uniform adaptive-optimizer disadvantage. PS-DA-SGD uses Adam parameter scaling despite its name.

rows.subject: VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizer test accuracy; CIFAR-100 top-1 test accuracy with train loss in parentheses.
rows.measure: Top-1 test accuracy; train loss in parentheses
rows.note: The paper states that learning-rate-free methods tend toward lower accuracy in these VGG experiments, primarily due to overfitting. The reported methods do not isolate the limited-tuning comparison specified by V4.
rows.check: Missing SGD baseline: 64.7% accuracy, training loss 0.038. All recorded adaptive methods have lower accuracy, 48.3–62.1%. D-Adapt Adam, Prodigy and PS-DA-SGD also have lower training loss than SGD. The restricted tuning protocol in V4 is not established.

rows.subject: ViT-Tiny
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizer ImageNet top-1 accuracy without weight decay.
rows.value: Adam 72.0; COCOB 0.14; LDoG 4.29; D-Adapt Adam 70.5; Prodigy 68.3; PS-SPS 42.0; PS-DA-SGD 39.3
rows.note: The paper describes Adam as a hand-tuned baseline and says PS-DA-SGD and D-Adapt Adam are comparable to Adam among learning-rate-free methods. The table is flattened; the method-to-value alignment follows the printed method and column ordering.
rows.check: PS-DA-SGD accuracy is 73.6%, not 39.3%. Missing SGD baseline: 18.9%. Adam, D-Adapt Adam, Prodigy and both proposed methods outperform SGD; COCOB and LDoG underperform it. Section 6.3 attributes the steepest-descent results to optimization failure, so this is not an isolated generalization-gap comparison.

rows.subject: ViT-Tiny
rows.operation_detail: Compared ImageNet top-1 accuracy with weight decay regularization.
rows.note: The paper says the performance gap between methods decreases when weight decay is enabled.
rows.check: All methods use adaptive gradients; there is no SGD comparator establishing V4's disadvantage or its recovery through decoupled weight decay. Section 6.3 also distinguishes other methods' reported results from the authors' own PS-DA-SGD experiment; do not assume every value is a newly run comparison.

rows.note: The authors report suboptimal fine-tuning performance for D-Adapt Adam and Prodigy, attributing it to relatively large estimated learning rates.
rows.check: Semantic-segmentation fine-tuning is outside V4's named benchmarks, and this row compares adaptive methods without SGD. The values measure optimizer performance, not the specified adaptive-versus-SGD effect.

rows.subject: Swin-T
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizer mean intersection-over-union on ADE20K.
rows.value: Adam 18.6; COCOB 41.4; LDoG 41.4; D-Adapt Adam 41.8; Prodigy 44.1; PS-SPS 43.8; PS-DA-SGD 44.0

rows.subject: SimCLR with ResNet-18 backbone

rows.value: Adam 76.0; COCOB 66.4; LDoG 74.5; D-Adapt Adam 69.0; Prodigy 76.9; PS-SPS 76.7; PS-DA-SGD 73.5

rows.check: This is self-supervised representation learning, with an incompletely described downstream accuracy evaluation, rather than V4's specified classification-training comparison. The recorded adaptive-only comparison does not establish an adaptive-versus-SGD generalization disadvantage.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-100, VGG-19 without batch normalization or weight decay; reported tuning procedure
relationships.reason: R2 plus the omitted SGD baseline show every recorded adaptive method below SGD's 64.7% accuracy; several attain lower training loss. This supports the optimizer ordering, although the limited-tuning condition is unverified.
relationships.display_finding: Reported adaptive accuracies fall below SGD's 64.7% despite lower training losses for several methods, but verification and tuning restrictions remain unresolved.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-100, ResNet-32: COCOB, LDoG, D-Adapt Adam and Prodigy versus SGD
relationships.reason: R1 plus the omitted baseline show these existing adaptive methods at 50.1–66.4%, below SGD's 66.7%; Prodigy also has slightly lower training loss. The tuning restriction is unverified.
relationships.display_finding: Reported accuracies for the specified adaptive methods trail SGD, despite slightly lower Prodigy training loss, but the comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-100, ResNet-32: hand-tuned Adam versus SGD
relationships.reason: R1 plus the omitted baseline show Adam achieving 68.3% versus SGD's 66.7%, with similar training losses, qualifying the disadvantage by optimizer and architecture.
relationships.display_finding: Adam reportedly exceeded SGD accuracy with similar training losses, but this comparison remains unverified.

relationships.condition: ImageNet, ViT-Tiny without weight decay: Adam, D-Adapt Adam and Prodigy versus SGD
relationships.reason: Corrected R3 plus the omitted baseline show 68.3–72.0% for these adaptive methods versus 18.9% for SGD. The text attributes SGD's poor result to optimization failure; adaptive methods have the practical advantage in this setting.
relationships.display_finding: Adaptive methods reportedly exceeded SGD substantially, with SGD's poor result attributed to optimization failure, but these comparisons remain unverified.
